summary: Edgartown's inner-harbor light, lit 1828 on a pier; the cast-iron tower standing today came from Ipswich in 1939. Town-owned since 2014, run by the Martha's Vineyard Museum.

structures.note: Cast-iron cylindrical tower moved by barge from Ipswich in 1939; the Gazette and the nomination date it to 1875, LighthouseFriends to 1881
Combination dwelling and light on pilings and then a pier; the house and lantern were torn down by the Coast Guard in 1939

access.note: The Museum keeps the doors open during visiting hours, with a keeper present. Closed for the 2026 season; reopening spring 2027 per the Museum. Parking limited on North Water Street; VTA buses drop off on Church Street, about 15 minutes' walk.

facts.agency: Town of Edgartown (owner since 2014, by GSA transfer); Martha's Vineyard Museum (steward)

events.note: Combination dwelling and light built on a platform/pilings at the harbor entrance; Congress approved funds (LighthouseFriends $5,500; nomination $4,400)
Keeper Pease's diary: Captain John Akin lighted the lamps on 15 October 1828 (LighthouseFriends)
1,500-foot wooden walkway built at a cost of $2,500 (LighthouseFriends)
Rotten wooden pilings replaced by a stone pier (LighthouseFriends)
Stone breakwater topped by a wooden walkway, $4,700 (nomination; LighthouseFriends)
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaced the old lamps and reflectors (LighthouseFriends; USLHS record)
Cast-iron cylindrical tower built (nomination; Gazette 2014). LighthouseFriends says 1881, at Crane's Beach, Ipswich
Storage shed added; 1896 iron oil house; 1908 fog bell (LighthouseFriends)
Great Hurricane of 1938 inflicted significant damage (LighthouseFriends; Gazette: badly damaged)
Coast Guard tore down the dwelling and lantern after taking over the lights (LighthouseFriends)
Cast-iron tower barged from Ipswich, minus its brick lining (LighthouseFriends), and set on the harbor site (nomination: floated by barge)
Lot adjacent to the light sold to the Town of Edgartown (nomination)
Thirty-year lease granted to the Martha's Vineyard Historical Society (LighthouseFriends)
Children's Memorial dedicated 14 July 2001 (LighthouseFriends); the Museum now counts more than 1,100 engraved stones
$250,000 from the Community Preservation Act; $80,000 staircase; first opened to the public for climbing (LighthouseFriends)
GSA transfer of ownership to the Town of Edgartown, announced January 2014; Museum continues as steward; cost about $1 (Vineyard Gazette)

corrections.why: The record's 1828 build is the first combination dwelling and light, lost in 1939. The cast-iron tower standing now dates from 1875 (nomination; Gazette), though LighthouseFriends gives 1881.

corrections.proposed: Town of Edgartown (owner); Martha's Vineyard Museum (steward)
corrections.why: The Town of Edgartown took the deed in January 2014 (Vineyard Gazette); the Museum continues as steward (Museum page).
The USLHS record gives the tower as 45 feet (13.7 m); the nomination gives it as 45 feet above water.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1828 build date belongs to the first dwelling-light; the standing cast-iron tower is the one moved from Ipswich in 1939 and dated 1875 by the nomination and the Gazette.

notes_for_editor: Unresolved: (1) Congress's sum for the 1828 light, $4,400 (nomination) against $5,500 (LighthouseFriends); (2) cast-iron tower date and origin: 1875 (nomination, Gazette 2014, 'Essex Light' from Ipswich) against 1881 (LighthouseFriends, rear range light on Crane's Beach); the Ipswich range tower is not checked in any Light List or corpus text; (3) LighthouseFriends' page still says the Coast Guard owns the light and the Martha's Vineyard Historical Society manages it; the 2014 Gazette says the Town took the deed, and the Museum's page calls itself steward; (4) the Museum's page says the light is closed for the 2026 season; climbing is not stated on the Museum's page, while LighthouseFriends says it opened for climbing after 2007; the story says visiting is through the Museum only; (5) the record's characteristic Fl R 6s is LighthouseFriends' 'flashing red every six seconds' but no Light List was read; (6) the 1878 to 1880s lens and first-lighting details, and the 1892 to 1908 additions, are LighthouseFriends only; (7) the 1934 newspaper is quoted second hand via LighthouseFriends; (8) the keeper Pease scandal is LighthouseFriends' account of a local paper, not read in the original; (9) the 1938 hurricane damage is given by LighthouseFriends and the Gazette, not by a weather record; (10) LHB 1895, 1897 and 1900 entries were located by matching the printed page indexes; page numbers 54, 49 and 50 match the report indexes. Checked on page images and the Gazette page in the fact-check (2026-10-22): the 1895 (scan 237, item 134), 1897 (scan 301, item 154) and 1900 (scan 60) Light-House Board entries were located by full-text search of the Internet Archive volumes, not by the printed indexes, and are cited by scan page. The Vineyard Gazette page (2014) carries a reader comment, by a writer who said the paper's own 1938 reports showed the building had been condemned that summer, that the 1938 hurricane did little or no damage; the story states this as a disagreement with the article's 'badly damaged'. The same page carries a reader correction for the Ipswich light's location (Crane Beach); the Gazette replied that the story had been updated, and the cached copy read here still reads 'Essex Light'. The nomination's 2 1/2-story dwelling and LighthouseFriends' two-story dwelling are both given. The 1842 description of Crocker's keeping is LighthouseFriends' transcription of his report, and the story paraphrases it rather than the whole passage.
